Hello,

I'm not sure if I understood the concept of FTR and PAZ right and would like to ask some questions.

Here's my take on FTRs (any comments and corrections are very appreciated):

1.FTRs are basically levels where one could expect enough supply or demand to drive price in a certain anticipated direction (i.e. to the next lower/upper FTR). So an FTR by definition must be a DBR, RBD, DBD or RBR. Is that correct?

2. An FTR not only has meaning when price gets there for the first time and bounces of it, but also when it gets engulfed and switches sides (e.g. from supply to demand).

But what does the term 'Failure to Return' exactly mean? Does it mean that the level was formed during price's failed attempt to get to the previous supply/demand level? If that is the case then two consecutive FTRs must by definition have a PAZ between them. Because if price would have made it to the previous FTR, it wouldn't be a 'failed' attempt in the first place, right? And it would explain why Pedini has not highlighted this yellow level in the chart below. Or am I just seeing things here?

So when an FTR gets engulfed it is a hint that price may reach for the next FTR, which gives us a nice target. So if after the engulfing price retraces to the now broken FTR, we get a great opportunity for an entry because we can assume that the former resistance now acts as support (or vice versa). From this perspective the concept of FTR gives us everything we need: a pretty sure shot entry, stop loss and target level.

Is that what FTRs are all about?

I hope I did not make it too complicated. Thanks for your help!

Here's how I am marking in the PAZs, based on my current understanding. I'm leaving out cpPAZ until I've got a handle on the FTR PAZ. I'm using the same chart area as above, so we've consistency. Peds, am I getting there?

1. First I mark in the FTRs I see. These I take to be an engulf (a new high in this case) showing intent to go higher, then the fail to go lower. It does not become a true FTR until price then moves higher than the initial higher high. So, for example, z does not qualify as an FTR as y is a few pips lower than x. (it is a cpPAZ edge, but I'm not going near those yet). I've used a little red ellipse to show the tips of the FTRs.

2. I then mark in the demand zones (or supply if moving down) which the FTRs represent. My indi marks those created above current price blue, and those below as pink). These are going to become the targets on the way down - the FTB to the FTR, essentially.

3. Then it's a case of watching what price does:

The engulf at 1 means expect price to go to 2 (engulf 1 also engulfs an FL to the left of the top elipse, and should have you primed and ready for point A to happen - it is ignored demand becoming supply - an SR flip).

The engulf at 3 means expect price to go to 4

The engulf at 5 means expect price to go to 6, whichever PAZ edge that leads to next. If you were sharp, you could maybe get in at B.

And see how the influence continues..

Here I tryed to draw some PAZ and FTR, any comment and suggestion is welcome.

If I understand correctly, one option to trade PAZ and FTR is: once a previous FTR is engulfed, we entered in a new PAZ between 2 FTRs. In my view a FTR is created when something (a previous High/Low, a Key Level, a previous FTR, a previous SD zone like RBR/DBD) gets engulfed and there is a pullback.

I think that most of the FLs are FTR too, because they form when a SR level gets engulfed and in the flag there is actually a pullback, an attempt to return to the origin of the move, so we can call it FTR.

But why not all FL are FTR? Well, if I understand FLs, most of the times a flag forms after a SR level gets engulfed, so we can call it FTR, but in some FLs the flag forms BEFORE the SR gets engulfed, so this flag has not yet engulfed something right now, so we can't call it FTR, in this case the real FTR is the FTB to the flag limit. Is this a FTR? No, because no engulf.
